title: Unit 1 Super Review (Days 1-15)
description: Comprehensive review covering everything from linear systems and Gaussian elimination through Cramer's Rule: RREF & free variables, matrix operations, linear transformations, the Invertibility Theorem, elementary matrices, inverse matrices, LU decomposition, and determinants. 20 questions pulled per attempt from a pool of 100.

questions.prompt: Swapping two rows of an augmented matrix changes the solution set of the system.
explanations: Row operations (including swaps) never change the solution set — that's the whole reason we're allowed to use them to solve systems.

questions.prompt: A system in RREF has at most one pivot per row.
explanations: By definition, each nonzero row of RREF has exactly one leading 1 (pivot), and it's the only pivot in that row.

questions.prompt: If a row of the augmented matrix reduces to [0  0  0 | 5], the system is inconsistent.
explanations: That row says 0 = 5, a contradiction — no values of the variables can satisfy it.

questions.prompt: A variable whose column has no pivot in RREF is called a _____ variable.
questions.explanation: Pivot (leading/basic) variables correspond to pivot columns; everything else is free.

questions.prompt: The RREF of a system's augmented matrix is [[1, 0, 3 | 7], [0, 1, -2 | 4]] for variables x, y, z (z is free). If z = t, what is x in terms of t?
questions.explanation: Row 1 reads x + 3z = 7, so x = 7 - 3z = 7 - 3t.

questions.prompt: A consistent system has more unknowns than equations, and every equation is independent (full row rank). What must be true of its solution set?
choices: It cannot be determined without more information
explanations: More unknowns than (independent) equations always leaves at least one free variable.
The system is given as consistent, so 'no solution' is ruled out.
It CAN be determined: full row rank with more unknowns than equations always forces at least one free variable.

questions.prompt: Solve: x + y = 5 and x − y = 1. What is x?
questions.explanation: Adding the two equations: 2x = 6, so x = 3 (and then y = 2).

questions.prompt: Every matrix has a unique RREF.
explanations: No matter which sequence of row operations you use, you always land on the same RREF.

questions.prompt: The number of pivots in a matrix's RREF is called its rank.
explanations: Rank is defined exactly this way: the number of pivot positions (equivalently, pivot columns).

questions.prompt: Two systems that have the same solution set (reachable from one another by row operations) are called _____ systems.
questions.explanation: 'Equivalent' is the standard term — the systems can look different but share every solution.

questions.prompt: In the single equation x + 2y − z = 6, y and z are free. If y = s and z = t, what is x in terms of s and t?
questions.explanation: Solve for the pivot variable x: x = 6 - 2y + z = 6 - 2s + t.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the three elementary row operations?
choices: Multiply a row by a nonzero scalar
Add a multiple of one row to another
explanations: This is a legal elementary row operation.
This is a legal elementary row operation (the scalar must be nonzero so it's reversible).
This is a legal elementary row operation.

questions.prompt: A system can have a free variable in its RREF and still have no solution.
explanations: Free/pivot status comes from the coefficient columns alone. If some OTHER row reduces to [0 0 ... 0 | nonzero], the system is inconsistent regardless of any free variables elsewhere.

questions.prompt: Solve: 2x + 3y = 12 and x − y = 1. What is y?
questions.explanation: From the second equation, x = 1 + y. Substituting: 2(1+y) + 3y = 12, so 5y = 10, y = 2.

questions.prompt: If two augmented matrices are row equivalent, they represent systems with the same solution set.
explanations: Row equivalence means one was reached from the other by row operations, which never change the solution set.
Check the (1,2) entry again: 2 + (-1) = 1, not 3.
Check the (2,1) entry again: 3 + 2 = 5, not 1.
Entries were subtracted where they should be added, or mismatched.
Every entry must be scaled by 2, not just the first column.
Every entry must be scaled by 2, not just the second column.
The bottom row was left unscaled.
The bottom row's entries are swapped — recompute row 2 of A times each column of B.
This looks like an entrywise product, not matrix multiplication.
Rows and columns are mixed up — recompute using row·column.

questions.prompt: Using the same A and B (A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]], B = [[0, -1], [2, 1]]), what is BA? (Compare it to AB above.)
explanations: That's AB, not BA — order matters, and this problem asks for BA.
The rows and columns are transposed from the correct answer.
The signs are flipped from the correct answer.

questions.prompt: (AB)ᵀ = AᵀBᵀ.
explanations: The correct identity reverses the order: (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ.

questions.explanation: Transposing a product reverses the order of the factors.

questions.prompt: Matrix multiplication is associative: (AB)C = A(BC).
explanations: Matrix multiplication is always associative, even though it isn't commutative.

questions.prompt: If AB is the zero matrix, then A must be the zero matrix or B must be the zero matrix.
explanations: Unlike real numbers, matrices can be zero divisors — e.g. A = [[0,1],[0,0]] and B = [[0,1],[0,0]] are both nonzero, but AB = [[0,0],[0,0]].

questions.prompt: C is a 2×3 matrix. What are the dimensions of Cᵀ (rows × columns)?
questions.explanation: Transposing swaps rows and columns: a 2×3 matrix becomes 3×2.

questions.prompt: For an m×n matrix A and an n×p matrix B, what are the dimensions of the product AB?
explanations: n×n would only be right if m = p = n; in general the product is m×p.
m×n is the shape of A itself, not the product.
The order is reversed — it's m×p, not p×m.

questions.prompt: A + B is only defined when A and B have the same dimensions.
explanations: Matrix addition is entrywise, so the matrices must line up entry-for-entry — same number of rows and columns.

questions.prompt: For square matrices, A² means A multiplied by itself using matrix multiplication (not each entry squared).
explanations: A² = A·A using matrix multiplication — squaring entries individually is a different (and much less useful) operation.

questions.prompt: A linear transformation T sends T(e1) = (2, 0) and T(e2) = (0, 3). What is its standard matrix?
explanations: The images become the COLUMNS in order, not the rows.
This puts both images into one row instead of separate columns.
The order of e1 and e2's images is swapped.

questions.prompt: What is the standard matrix of a 90° counterclockwise rotation in R²?
explanations: This is the matrix for a 90° CLOCKWISE rotation instead.
This is a reflection across the x-axis, not a rotation.
This is a reflection across the y-axis, not a rotation.

questions.prompt: What is the standard matrix of the projection onto the x-axis, T(x,y) = (x, 0)?
explanations: This is the projection onto the y-axis instead.
This is the identity transformation — it doesn't project onto anything.
This doesn't fix the x-coordinate the way a projection onto the x-axis should.

questions.prompt: What is the standard matrix of a reflection across the y-axis, T(x,y) = (-x, y)?
explanations: That's a reflection across the x-axis instead.
That's not a reflection across either axis.
That's a 180° rotation, not a reflection across the y-axis.

questions.prompt: If T is a linear transformation, then T(0) = 0.
explanations: T(0) = T(0·v) = 0·T(v) = 0 by the scalar (homogeneity) property of linearity.

questions.prompt: T(x, y) = (x + 1, y) is a linear transformation.
explanations: A linear transformation must send 0 to 0, but T(0,0) = (1,0) ≠ (0,0), so this fails immediately.

questions.prompt: T(x, y) = (3x, x + y). What is T(2, 1)? Give your answer as an ordered pair like (a, b).
T(x, y) = (x − y, 2y). What is T(4, 1)?
The columns of a linear transformation T's standard matrix are:
choices: the images T(e1), T(e2), …, T(en), in order
explanations: Eigenvectors are a completely different (later) topic — not what builds the standard matrix.
The domain is the space T acts on, not a description of the matrix's columns.
The kernel is the set of vectors T sends to 0 — it's not the columns of the matrix.

questions.prompt: A transformation T: Rⁿ → Rᵐ is linear if and only if T(u+v) = T(u)+T(v) and T(cu) = _____ for every scalar c.
questions.explanation: This is the homogeneity condition: scaling the input scales the output by the same factor.

questions.prompt: Every linear transformation from Rⁿ to Rᵐ can be represented by some m×n matrix.
explanations: This is the Standard Matrix Theorem — the matrix's columns are T(e1), …, T(en).

questions.prompt: A transformation scales the x-coordinate by 2 and leaves y unchanged: T(x,y) = (2x, y). What is its standard matrix?
explanations: This scales y instead of x.
This scales both coordinates by 2, but y should stay unchanged.
The rows/columns are mixed up.

questions.prompt: If det(A) ≠ 0, then A is invertible.
explanations: A nonzero determinant is one of the equivalent conditions in the Invertibility Theorem.

questions.prompt: If Ax = 0 has a nontrivial solution, then A is invertible.
explanations: A nontrivial solution to Ax=0 is exactly the signal that A is NOT invertible.

questions.prompt: An invertible n×n matrix is row equivalent to the n×n identity matrix.
explanations: Row equivalence to I is another one of the Invertibility Theorem's equivalent conditions.

questions.prompt: For an n×n matrix A, which of these is equivalent to saying A is NOT invertible?
choices: The columns of A are linearly independent
Ax = 0 has only the trivial solution
explanations: This describes an INVERTIBLE matrix.
This describes an INVERTIBLE matrix.
This describes an INVERTIBLE matrix.

questions.prompt: A is invertible if and only if the columns of A are linearly _____.
questions.explanation: Linear independence of the columns is one of the Invertibility Theorem's equivalent conditions.

questions.prompt: If A is invertible, then Ax = b has a unique solution for every b.
explanations: x = A⁻¹b always exists and is unique when A is invertible.

questions.prompt: A singular (non-invertible) n×n matrix has n pivot columns.
explanations: A singular matrix has FEWER than n pivot columns — that's exactly why it's singular.

questions.prompt: An n×n matrix has fewer than n pivot columns in its RREF. Is it invertible? Answer yes or no.
questions.explanation: Fewer than n pivot columns means A is NOT row equivalent to the identity, so A is not invertible.

questions.prompt: For an n×n matrix A, which of these is NOT equivalent to 'A is invertible'?
choices: The rows of A are linearly independent
The columns of A span Rⁿ
A has at least one free variable in Ax = 0
A is row equivalent to the identity matrix
explanations: This IS equivalent to A being invertible.
This IS equivalent to A being invertible.
This IS equivalent to A being invertible.

questions.prompt: Every square matrix is invertible.
explanations: Only square matrices with nonzero determinant (full rank) are invertible — plenty of square matrices are singular.

questions.prompt: The matrix [[1, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0], [-3, 0, 1]] is a 3×3 elementary matrix.
explanations: It's the identity matrix after exactly one row operation: add -3·R1 to R3.

questions.prompt: The matrix [[1, -2], [0, 1]] is a 2×2 elementary matrix.
explanations: It's the identity after exactly one row operation: add -2·R2 to R1.

questions.prompt: The elementary matrix [[1, 0], [0, 5]] came from which row operation on the identity matrix?
explanations: Adding a multiple of one row to another wouldn't leave R1 unchanged and only scale R2.
A row swap wouldn't produce a 5 on the diagonal.
This would put the 5 in the (1,1) position, not (2,2).

questions.prompt: The inverse of an elementary matrix is also an elementary matrix.
explanations: Each type of elementary row operation (swap, scale, add-a-multiple) is undone by another elementary row operation of the same type.

questions.prompt: Left-multiplying A by an elementary matrix E performs a _____ operation on A.
questions.explanation: Elementary matrices encode row operations; multiplying on the right instead performs column operations.

questions.prompt: E = [[1, 0], [3, 1]] represents 'add 3·R1 to R2'. What is E⁻¹?
explanations: That's E itself, not its inverse — applying the same operation twice doesn't undo it.
The multiplier should be negated, not inverted.
This isn't even a valid elementary matrix for this operation.

questions.prompt: A product of elementary matrices is always invertible.
explanations: Each elementary matrix is invertible, and a product of invertible matrices is invertible.

questions.prompt: An elementary matrix representing 'swap R1 and R2' is its own:
explanations: A determinant is a number, not a matrix — this doesn't make sense as an answer.
The adjoint is a different construction entirely.
It's actually both its own transpose AND its own inverse here — 'transpose only' is too narrow.

questions.prompt: Matrix addition is commutative: A + B = B + A.
explanations: Matrix addition is entrywise, and ordinary number addition is commutative, so the entries add up the same way in either order.

questions.prompt: Matrix multiplication is commutative: AB = BA for all A, B.
explanations: Matrix multiplication is generally NOT commutative — order matters.

questions.prompt: If A and B are square and AB = I, then BA = I as well.
explanations: For square matrices, a one-sided inverse is automatically a two-sided inverse.

questions.prompt: (AB)⁻¹ = A⁻¹B⁻¹.
explanations: The correct identity reverses the order: (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹.

questions.explanation: Just like the transpose, inverting a product reverses the order of the factors.

questions.prompt: If A is invertible, then (Aᵀ)⁻¹ = (A⁻¹)ᵀ.
explanations: Transpose and inverse commute: (Aᵀ)⁻¹ = (A⁻¹)ᵀ always holds for invertible A.

questions.prompt: The zero matrix has an inverse.
explanations: The zero matrix has determinant 0, so it's never invertible.

questions.prompt: A = [[2, 1], [1, 1]] (det(A) = 1, so A⁻¹ = [[1, -1], [-1, 2]]) and b = (5, 3). Using x = A⁻¹b, what is x (the first coordinate)?
questions.explanation: x = A⁻¹b = (1·5 + (−1)·3, −1·5 + 2·3) = (2, 1), so the first coordinate is 2.

questions.prompt: The cancellation law AB = AC implies B = C for any nonzero matrix A.
explanations: Cancellation only works if A is INVERTIBLE, not merely nonzero — a singular nonzero A can still fail cancellation.

questions.prompt: In A = LU (no row swaps needed), L is lower triangular with 1's on the diagonal.
explanations: L records the row-reduction multipliers below a diagonal of 1's — that's the standard convention for LU.

questions.prompt: In A = LU, U is upper triangular.
explanations: U is exactly the row-echelon form reached by forward elimination — upper triangular by construction.

questions.prompt: Every square matrix has an LU decomposition without any row swaps.
explanations: Some matrices require a row swap during elimination, in which case you need a PLU decomposition instead.

questions.prompt: When row swaps are needed during elimination, we instead compute a _____ decomposition.
questions.explanation: The permutation matrix P records the swaps: A = PLU (or PA = LU).

questions.prompt: Why is it useful to compute an LU decomposition of A?
choices: To solve Ax = b efficiently for many different b vectors
To find the eigenvalues of A instantly
explanations: LU decomposition doesn't directly give eigenvalues — that's a different (later) topic.
LU decomposition has nothing to do with symmetry.
Transposing a matrix doesn't require LU decomposition at all.

questions.prompt: In a PLU decomposition, P is a permutation matrix.
explanations: P just reorders rows to record the row swaps used during elimination, so it's a permutation matrix (identity with rows reordered).

questions.prompt: The product of two upper triangular matrices (of the same size) is upper triangular.
explanations: Every entry below the diagonal of the product comes out to 0 — upper triangular matrices are closed under multiplication.

questions.prompt: To solve Ax = b using A = LU, what do you solve first?
explanations: You need y from Ly=b before you can use U at all.
This isn't a meaningful equation to solve first.
This isn't the right order — L comes first.

questions.prompt: Find the determinant: det([[3, 5], [2, 4]])
Find the determinant: det([[-2, 3], [4, 1]])
det(I) = 1 for an identity matrix of any size.
explanations: The identity matrix is triangular with all 1's on the diagonal, so its determinant is the product of the diagonal: 1.

questions.prompt: If a matrix has a row of all zeros, its determinant is 0.
explanations: Cofactor expansion along the zero row gives a sum of terms that are all multiplied by 0.

questions.prompt: Find the determinant of the lower-triangular matrix [[2, 0, 0], [1, 3, 0], [4, 5, 6]].
questions.explanation: For a triangular matrix, det is the product of the diagonal entries: 2 · 3 · 6 = 36.

questions.prompt: For an upper or lower triangular matrix, det(A) equals:
choices: the product of the diagonal entries
the sum of the diagonal entries
explanations: That would be the trace, not the determinant.
The determinant isn't simply the largest entry.
Only true if every diagonal entry happens to multiply to 1 — not a general rule.

questions.prompt: Find the determinant of the upper-triangular matrix [[1, 2, 3], [0, 1, 4], [0, 0, 1]].
questions.explanation: Product of the diagonal entries: 1 · 1 · 1 = 1.

questions.prompt: Swapping two rows of a matrix multiplies its determinant by -1.
explanations: A row swap is one of the elementary operations, and it's the one that flips the determinant's sign.

questions.prompt: The determinant is defined for non-square matrices too.
explanations: The determinant is only defined for square matrices.

questions.prompt: Expanding a determinant along a row or column using signed minors is called _____ expansion.
questions.explanation: This is the cofactor (Laplace) expansion method.

questions.prompt: det(AB) = det(A)·det(B).
explanations: This multiplicative property of the determinant holds for any two square matrices of the same size.

questions.prompt: det(A+B) = det(A) + det(B) in general.
explanations: There is no such addition rule for determinants — this fails for almost any example you try.

questions.prompt: A is 2×2 with det(A) = 3. What is det(2A)?
questions.explanation: det(kA) = kⁿdet(A) for n×n A. Here n=2, k=2: det(2A) = 2²·3 = 12.

questions.prompt: For an n×n matrix A and scalar k, det(kA) equals:
explanations: This forgets that EVERY row gets scaled by k, not just one.
This isn't how scaling interacts with determinants at all.
This is only correct when n = 2 specifically — not the general rule.

questions.prompt: det(Aᵀ) = det(A).
explanations: Transposing a matrix never changes its determinant — cofactor expansion along a row of A matches expansion along the corresponding column of Aᵀ.

questions.prompt: Adding a multiple of one row to another row changes the value of the determinant.
explanations: This is exactly the one elementary row operation that leaves the determinant unchanged.

questions.prompt: det(A) = 5. What is det(A⁻¹)?
questions.explanation: det(A⁻¹) = 1/det(A) = 1/5.

questions.prompt: A matrix with det(A) = 0 must have linearly dependent columns.
explanations: det(A) = 0 is one of the equivalent conditions in the Invertibility Theorem — it forces the columns to be linearly dependent.

questions.prompt: Cramer's Rule requires det(A) ≠ 0.
explanations: Cramer's Rule divides by det(A), so it only works when det(A) ≠ 0 (i.e., when A is invertible).

questions.prompt: Using Cramer's Rule, det(A) = 2 and det(Aₓ) = 8 (A with the x-column replaced by b). What is x?
questions.explanation: x = det(Aₓ)/det(A) = 8/2 = 4.

questions.prompt: Cramer's Rule works only for square systems.
explanations: Cramer's Rule relies on det(A), which only exists when A is square, so the method requires as many equations as unknowns.

questions.prompt: In Cramer's Rule, Aᵢ is the matrix A with column i replaced by _____.
questions.explanation: Aᵢ swaps in the right-hand-side vector b for column i.

questions.prompt: det(A⁻¹) = 1/det(A).
explanations: Since det(A)·det(A⁻¹) = det(A·A⁻¹) = det(I) = 1, it follows that det(A⁻¹) = 1/det(A).

questions.prompt: Using the adjoint formula A⁻¹ = (1/det(A))·adj(A): det(A) = 4 and adj(A) has entry 8 in position (1,1). What is (A⁻¹) in position (1,1)?
questions.explanation: (A⁻¹)₁₁ = adj(A)₁₁ / det(A) = 8/4 = 2.

questions.prompt: If det(A) = 0, Cramer's Rule still gives a valid unique solution via 0/0.
explanations: det(A) = 0 means A isn't invertible — Cramer's Rule simply doesn't apply, not that it gives a 0/0 answer.
